prompt.context: Our client is a zoo that is thinking about acquiring a famous zebra from an African preserve. It's a huge investment, but they believe the new zebra would be a great contribution to their animal community.
prompt.question: You have been engaged to help decide whether this is a good idea. What would you consider when trying to help your client make this decision?

clarifying_info.q: How many people visit the zoo annually?
What attendance benefit might the zebra bring?
clarifying_info.a: Another zoo that acquired a similar zebra had an 8% increase in attendance.
Acquisition cost: $235K; new facilities: $850K; transportation: $110K. All upfront costs are paid today.
Annual maintenance (food, health costs, additional trainers): $90K per year.

clarifying_info.q: What discount rate should we use?
clarifying_info.a: Discount rate is 20%. Annual costs and benefits begin next year and are sustained in perpetuity (assume the zebra lives forever to simplify).

exhibits.title: Market Research: Possible Attendance Increases
exhibits.shows: A table and bar chart showing four possible attendance increase scenarios with associated annual revenue from increased attendance and their probabilities, plus a summary of expected additional annual revenue and total expected annual revenue.

framework: Quantify upfront investment costs: acquisition, facilities, transportation
Estimate annual revenue benefit from increased attendance (use comparable zoo as proxy)
Calculate NPV using perpetuity formula: NPV = -Upfront Costs + (Annual Benefit - Annual Cost) / Discount Rate
Perform break-even analysis: find minimum attendance increase needed for NPV ≥ 0
Use market research (Exhibit 1) to assess probability of achieving break-even
Evaluate risk mitigation: assess whether the insurance contract creates value
Bonus: evaluate ancillary investment opportunities (GWF exhibit)

questions.prompt: Calculate the NPV of the zebra acquisition using the 8% attendance increase assumption.
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify annual benefit from attendance increase, subtract annual costs, then apply perpetuity formula net of upfront costs. NPV > 0 means the acquisition is financially justified under this assumption.

math.setup: Annual benefit = 300,000 visitors x $15 admission x 8% increase. Upfront costs = $235K + $850K + $110K. Annual costs = $90K. NPV = -Upfront + (Annual Benefit - Annual Cost) / Discount Rate.
math.answer: NPV = +$155,000. The acquisition appears financially positive under the 8% attendance increase assumption.

questions.prompt: Zoo Co. is concerned that the 8% attendance increase from the comparable zoo may not apply. What analysis would you perform? What is the break-even attendance increase?
questions.guidance: Candidate should recommend a sensitivity/break-even analysis. They should solve for the revenue level that makes NPV = 0, then back out the required attendance increase percentage.

math.setup: Set NPV = 0: -$1,195,000 + (Revenue - $90,000) / 0.20 = 0. Solve for Revenue, then solve for % increase = Revenue / (300,000 x $15).
steps: Revenue = $239,000 + $90,000 = $329,000 (required additional revenue to break even)
math.answer: Break-even attendance increase = 7.3%. The zoo needs at least a 7.3% increase in attendance to justify the investment.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1 (market research), assess whether the zoo is likely to achieve break-even. Then evaluate the insurance contract: the insurer offers to top up annual revenue to $250,000 if attendance increases are ≤ 5%, in exchange for a premium of 1% of total expected annual revenues. Is this a good deal?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note that Exhibit 1 shows 60% probability of attendance increases ≤ 5% (20% at 3%, 40% at 5%), which are both below the 7.3% break-even — making the investment risky. For insurance: compare annual premium cost to expected annual benefit from the contract.

math.setup: Annual premium cost = 1% of expected total annual revenues. Annual expected benefit = (payout when 3% scenario) x P(3%) + (payout when 5% scenario) x P(5%). Payout = $250,000 - actual revenue in that scenario.
steps: Cost ($47,520) > Benefit ($33,000), so insurance is NOT a good deal
math.answer: Expected annual cost of insurance ($47,520) exceeds expected annual benefit ($33,000). The insurance contract does not create value for the zoo.

questions.prompt: BONUS (if time permits): The Global Wildlife Federation will pay the zoo $500K after hosting its endangered insect exhibit for one year, and the exhibit will generate an additional $280K in revenue. Setup costs are $655K. Is this exhibit worthwhile?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate a simple one-period NPV with all revenues occurring after year 1.

math.setup: NPV = -Setup Cost + (GWF payment + incremental revenue) / (1 + discount rate)
math.answer: NPV = -$5,000. The exhibit is marginally unprofitable and not worth pursuing.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors beyond the financial analysis should the zoo consider when deciding whether to acquire the zebra?

categories.name: Strategic / Mission
ideas: Competitive positioning vs. other regional zoos

categories.name: Operational
ideas: Animal welfare and compatibility with existing animal community

categories.name: Risk
ideas: Zebra health and mortality risk (animal may not live as expected)
Attendance increase may be lower than comparable zoo due to market differences

categories.name: Alternative uses of capital
ideas: Other animal acquisitions with higher expected attendance uplift
Marketing spend to drive attendance without acquisition cost

recommendation: The zebra acquisition is unlikely to be a good idea given the market research. While the NPV is positive under an assumed 8% attendance increase, the break-even analysis shows a 7.3% increase is required, and market research indicates a 60% probability that attendance grows by 5% or less — well below break-even.
The insurance contract offered does not create value: the annual premium cost ($47,520) exceeds the expected annual benefit ($33,000), so it should not be accepted as structured.
risks: Actual attendance increase may fall below break-even (60% probability based on market research)
Insurance contract is overpriced and does not adequately hedge downside risk
Upfront capital of ~$1.2M is at risk if attendance gains are insufficient
next_steps: Negotiate with the insurance company to either increase the revenue guarantee threshold or reduce the premium to create a value-positive contract
Conduct additional market research specific to this zoo's customer base before committing capital
Explore whether alternative exhibits (e.g., GWF insect exhibit) could generate better risk-adjusted returns, and optimize the investment portfolio accordingly
